utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, it appears from the witness's 2 answers to the previous questions that he has not seen these 3 documents before, that he has had no connection with them, that 4 they, in fact, come from another police station and, therefore, 5 they cannot be admitted through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a rather extraordinary objection, 8 not only in terms of its timing, but in terms of its content. 9 These are documents which were provided to the Prosecution by 10 the Defence and which they represented to us had come from the 11 Prijedor police and for which they had seen the originals. The Court will recall very early in this trial 13 documents were admitted on the very basis of that representation 14 by the Defence. I refer specifically to the mobilization list 15 which was introduced and admitted quite some time ago and 16 presented to a witness who knew nothing about it. But based on 17 those representations by the Defence, the document was, in fact, 18 admitted. This is a document for which a foundation has been 20 laid, and that is that it came from the Prijedor police, the 21 same organisation which provided the documents which have been 22 the subject of some discussion for several days this week. Any 23 objection about this witness's knowledge or lack of knowledge 24 could only go to the weight to be given this document as well as 25 the other documents. I have no problem with the argument that, in so far as 27 all these documents are concerned, there may be a serious 28 question about the weight, but clearly this particular document or this particular set of documents provided by the Prijedor police shed light on the weight to be given the other documents. 4 MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, if I might just respond to that? The mobilization lists to which Mr. Tieger referred were presented through an expert witness to comment on the lists. That is a quite different situation from a witness of fact commenting on something which he has never, in fact, seen before. I am not objecting in principle to these documents, but only to the fact that they cannot be brought in through this witness because he cannot comment on them. 12 MR. TIEGER: Your Honour, if I may say, they are not being brought in through this witness, they are being presented to this witness and brought into the foundation laid by the Defence. 15 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: OK. I will overrule your objection. It will go to the weight. 357A and B are still in. The only problem that you will have, of course, since he did not prepare these entries, I do not know how you are going to impeach any prior testimony or whatever that he may have given. I do not know what your intent was, but in any case let us see where you are going. Mr. Vujanovic, thank you. Mr. Vujanovic, can you hear me? 24 THE WITNESS: Yes, I can. 25 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: You may continue. 26 MR. TIEGER: Thank you, your Honour. 27 Q. Mr. Vujanovic, looking again at the patrol report on the left side of the page of PC1, that indicates, does it not, that it is a patrol report for a shift of September 1st 1992? Is that right, sir? I did not hear any answer. 3 A. I have not understood the question. Would you please be so kind as to repeat it? 5 Q. Certainly. I am directing your attention to the patrol report on the left side of the page and simply asking whether it indicates that is a patrol for September 1st 1992. 8 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: It appears we have lost the sound. 9 THE WITNESS: The sound was lost. 10 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Vujanovic, would you please repeat your answer? We did not have the sound. 12 THE WITNESS: Since I am working on these things and I know of such documents, patrol instructions and so on, but these documents that I have before me I am not familiar with, nor am I competent or authorised to provide any kind of information regarding those documents. 17 MR. TIEGER: Let me quickly direct your attention then to the page marked "PC2". On the left side of the page we see a patrol report. The date on that patrol report on this document is September 3rd 1992, correct? 21 A. September 3rd 1992, yes. 22 Q. The hours indicated are 17.30 to 600? 23 A. From 17 to 600. 24 Q. In the area of Vidovici? 25 A. I am not familiar with that. 26 Q. That is what the document says, however, right? 27 A. I do not even know whether Vidovici exists in that region there. 28 Q. The particular duty is reconnaissance duty; that is listed at the top of the document? 2 A. Yes. 3 Q. The leader of the patrol of a total of six people is Dusko Tadic? 5 A. That is what it says in this document. 6 Q. So this document shows Dusko Tadic patrolling in Vidovici, whether or not it exists, at the same time that your work list has him working at the bus and railway station in central Prijedor? 10 A. Could I please receive an extract from the work list? 11 Q. Please, that is 78A. What time does your work list, Exhibit 78A, say that Dusko Tadic was working at the railway and bus station? 14 A. On September 3rd he worked from 21 to 6 hours in the morning. 15 Q. According to the work list? 16 A. Yes. 17 MR. TIEGER: Your Honour, that is all I have. 18 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Miss de Bertodano? 19 MISS DE BERTODANO: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 21 Q. Mr. Vujanovic, if I could take you back to the daily schedule which was marked Prosecution 356, and if a copy of that could be put in front of you? If we look at the note in the top right-hand corner, you told us that you thought that would have been written on later, is that right? 26 A. Yes, the regular daily schedule does not include any such remarks, so this was written in later. 28 Q. You cannot see who has signed that part at the top right-hand corner? 2 A. According to this signature, I cannot tell who signed it. 3 Q. You also pointed out that there was another stamp at the bottom right-hand side of the page. Do you see that? 5 A. Yes, I do. 6 Q. Would that stamp normally be on a daily schedule? 7 A. In the lower right-hand corner it is normal and not in the upper right-hand corner. 9 Q. Would the schedule normally be signed by someone? 10 A. The daily schedule is signed by the station Commander. 11 Q. Can you see a signature of that sort on that daily schedule? 12 A. Because the copy is highly illegible I cannot tell whose signature it is. 14 Q. But do you see that there is a signature there? 15 A. I do, I do, yes. 16 Q. In your evidence you suggested that there might be a confusion between 21st and 12th August, is that right? 18 A. According to the schedule for the date of 21st, it says that Dusko Tadic was working from 6 to 1400 hours. 20 Q. Mr. Vujanovic, I am afraid we lost some sound there so I am going to ask you to repeat your previous answer. I had asked you about the possible confusion between 12th and 21st August. 23 A. A technical error in typing was probably made; instead of "12" the typist typed "21" because, according to the date, the 12th, it appears that Dusko Tadic worked from 9 to 21 hours. 26 Q. I would like to draw your attention to some other names on that list. Could you look at the 14 to 21 hour shift at the fourth police region and the person listed at No. 5? Can you read out what you can of his name there? 2 A. Boro. 3 Q. Can you see a first letter of the surname? 4 A. The first letter is a P or an R. 5 Q. If I could ask for Exhibit 74A to be put in front of you again. If I could draw your attention to the name at 320 on that list. 7 A. I see it. 8 Q. What is the name there, so far as you can read it? 9 A. Boro. 10 Q. Again can you read an initial for the surname? 11 A. P. 12 Q. If you go along the schedule against that name to 12th August, can you tell me when and where this person was working on 12th August from that duty list? 15 A. On the basis of this work list and the daily schedule, it emerges that this person worked with Dusko Tadic in the Fourth District. 18 Q. What hours was he working according to the duty list? 19 A. From 1400 to 2100 hours. 20 Q. If you could look along a few boxes to his entry for 21st August, what hours was he working on 21st August? 22 A. Does the question refer to Boro? 23 Q. Yes, it does. 24 A. On 21st August he worked in the Fourth District from 6.00 to 1400 hours. 26 Q. Thank you. If we could go back to the daily schedule and if you would look again with regard to the Fourth Police Region, the shift from 2100 hours to 06 hours, and the seventh name listed on that shift? 2 A. Simo. 3 Q. Can you read the first letter of the surname? 4 A. S. 5 Q. On Exhibit 74, the August duty book, can I ask you to look at the name at 321? 7 A. I see it. 8 Q. What is the name written there? 9 A. "Simo" it says. 10 Q. Again can you read the initial of the surname? 11 A. Also S. 12 Q. If you look along his duty shifts to his shift on 12th August, can you tell us what shift he was performing on that day, according to the duty list? 15 A. On the basis of the list, he was working from 2100 to 06 hours. 16 Q. Is that the same time as he is listed as working on the daily schedule? 18 A. Yes, it is the same. 19 Q. If we look along to 21st August on the duty list, what hours is he listed as working on 21st August? 21 A. For the person under 7, under No. 7? 22 Q. Yes, but I am asking you with regard to the August '92 duty list where he is at No. 321. 24 A. For August 21st he worked in the Fourth District from 1400 to 2100 hours. 26 Q. Thank you. If I could get you to turn back to the daily schedule and look at one more name. In the Fifth Police Region on the 1400 to 2100 hours shift, could you read me the name that you see at No. 3? 2 A. It applies to the Fifth Police District. 3 Q. That is right, yes, 1400 to 2100-hour shift, and the name No. 3 on that shift? 5 A. Miroslav. 6 Q. Can you read the first initial of the surname? 7 A. S. 8 Q. I think you may be reading at No. 4. If I could ask you to look at No. 3. 10 A. In the period from 1400 to 2100 hours? 11 Q. Yes, at No. 3 in the Fifth Police Region. 12 A. Miroslav? 13 Q. Yes, and the initial of the surname? 14 A. C. 15 Q. Thank you. 16 A. C. 17 Q. If we look to the August 1992 duty list and we look to No. 318 on that list? 19 A. I see it. 20 Q. Can you read the name that appears there? 21 A. Miroslav. 22 Q. And the initial of the surname, if you can see it? 23 A. I see it, C. 24 Q. If we look along his hours for August to 12th August, can you tell us what hours he was working on 12th August? 26 A. On 12th August he was working from 1400 to 2200 hours. 27 Q. If we look further along to 21st August, what hours was he working on that day? 1 A. On 21st August, from 6 to 1400 hours. 2 Q. Thank you very much. Those Exhibits can now be returned to the Registry. 4 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Tieger, do you have additional -- I am sorry. 6 MISS DE BERTODANO: I had not finished, your Honour. 7 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: I am just rushing you right along! I am sorry. 8 MISS DE BERTODANO: (To the witness): You were shown by Mr. Tieger some patrol warrants and you told us that you were not familiar with these warrants, is that right? 11 A. That is right. 12 Q. Were you familiar with anything that happened at Kozarac police station? 14 A. I had no contact with them. 15 Q. Do you know who wrote those warrants? 16 A. I do not know. 17 Q. Can you say whether they are genuine or not? 18 A. I cannot say anything. 19 Q. However, the records that you have shown us from Prijedor police station are based on a system, as you have outlined to us, and a system which you had worked at regularly during 1992, is that right? 23 A. Yes. 24 MISS DE BERTODANO: Nothing further, your Honour. 25 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Tieger? 26 MR. TIEGER: No, your Honour, nothing further. 27 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Is there any objection to Mr. Vujanovic being permanently excused? 1 MR. TIEGER: Yes, your Honour, there is. 2 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Vujanovic, you are free to leave. However, you are not permanently excused. You may be recalled for testimony. So, please keep in touch with Mr. Wladimiroff and, if it is necessary for you to return to give additional testimony before the Tribunal, we will tell you. Will you do that? 8 THE WITNESS: There is no problem whatsoever. If necessary I will be there. 10 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Thank you, Mr. Vujanovic. You are now excused. 12 THE WITNESS: You are welcome. (The witness withdrew). 14 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Well, the timing worked well. It is 10 minutes to 12.00. I understand you will hear something regarding Mr. Budimir at 12.00. We will stand in recess for lunch, but if you will let us now what you hear we will be here in the building. 19 MR. KAY: Your Honour, I heard slightly earlier that it would be 1.00 or after 1.00 o'clock from the Registry. Miss Featherstone had spoken directly to Mr. Marro. 22 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Bos told me 12.00. Where are we? 23 MR. KAY: Let them fight it out! 24 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: That is OK. You spoke last to Mr. Marro. 25 MISS FEATHERSTONE: I did, yes. He said 1.00 o'clock. 26 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: He said 1.00 o'clock. Does that pose a problem? We could still begin at 1.30. We will either begin with Mr. Budimir testifying via video link or we will not hear 1 any more testimony, as I understand it, this afternoon since you 2 do not have any more witnesses. They are coming this weekend 3 and then Mr. Budimir would come next week.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So 1.30 will work, if you hear at 1.00. If you 6 do not hear, of course, then we will be here and we will see 7 whether we will actually begin at 1.30 or whether we will have a 8 delay of waiting for a response. We do not want to lose too 9 much time because you have listed Mr. Budimir for three hours 10 and we do not want to wait too long. If we have not heard it 11 would be better for Mr. Budimir to be there available rather 12 than to lose that time and then have to use it next week, 13 because next week is pretty full. We will stand in recess until 1.30.
